album: The Shape of Jazz to Come
label: Atlantic
rationale: The rubric names this exact album as the borderline-avant case to argue as scope_call rather than auto-exclude. The case for: it is one of the most consequential jazz records ever made — Library of Congress National Recording Registry (2012), Grammy Hall of Fame (2015), all three Rolling Stone 500 lists — and its pianoless quartet is a lineage bridge out of bebop head-solo-head form that shaped Coltrane, Coleman Hawkins' heirs, and everything after; 'Lonely Woman' is a standard. The case against: Wikipedia and AllMusic both tag it free jazz, an excluded style; the council should judge whether 1959 Ornette is the canon's outer edge or outside it. John rules.

ballot.album: Ornette Coleman — The Shape of Jazz to Come (1959)

scope_check.boundary_note: The 1959 date is safely in range, but free-jazz/avant-garde classification is the decisive boundary: both Wikipedia (S1) and AllMusic (S2) tag it as free jazz, while the rubric explicitly identifies this exact record as a borderline avant-garde case requiring a scope ruling rather than automatic exclusion.

ballot.case_for: If John judges its retained pulse, melodic themes, blues-rooted material, and head-solo-head traces as sufficient post-bop continuity, this is an indispensable canon record. Coleman, Don Cherry, Charlie Haden, and Billy Higgins make the pianoless quartet a defining ensemble, and the record's liberation from chordal accompaniment made a foundational change in jazz improvisation and subsequent 1960s lineage. Its consensus is unusually broad: the dossier cites National Recording Registry induction, Grammy Hall of Fame recognition, and multiple Rolling Stone 500 appearances; "Lonely Woman" remains an emotionally immediate standard and a powerful discovery entry point.
ballot.case_against: The strongest objection is not quality but scope: this is widely understood as a founding free-jazz document, and both consulted overview sources explicitly classify it as free jazz/avant-garde jazz (S1, S2). Its rejection of fixed harmonic progression is a rupture from the post-bop/modal tradition, not merely an adventurous extension of it; admitting the origin-point record risks making the canon's exclusion of later free-jazz records difficult to apply consistently. The documentation establishes basic personnel and session facts but relies chiefly on Wikipedia and AllMusic, without original liner notes or a stronger sessionographic source, leaving some production detail unresolved.
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes that John make an explicit ruling on whether this melodic, pulse-based 1959 Ornette date is the permitted outer edge of post-bop or the excluded free-jazz threshold; if permitted, treat it as must-have.
